name: PT Merdeka Gold Resources Tbk

frontmatter.title: Merdeka Gold Resources: a scarce mine, fairly priced for its plan
frontmatter.summary: We initiate on Merdeka Gold Resources with a HOLD and a Rp4,971 target, -4.9% against the share price. Pani is a scarce asset — Indonesia's largest primary gold mine by resources, cheap to mine and about to triple output — but at Rp5,225 the equity already pays for gold a sixth above our through-cycle marker, and for a CIL build, a placement and a leverage peak that all have to go right.
thesis: The price needs gold around US$4,976/oz — about a sixth above the through-cycle marker the metals desk underwrites and well above spot — to earn its cost of capital; that is a plausible gold call rather than our base case.

Pani is a genuinely scarce asset — 5,200 koz of reserves estimated at US$2,300/oz, a low strip ratio, a fifteen-year plan and a cost structure that keeps life-of-mine AISC well under the deck gold price.

Output roughly triples into the CIL years, but the US$775.4m of capital in FY2027E, the placement that helps fund it and the 2.3x pre-placement leverage peak all have to land before the free cash flow does.
The bull case — gold above the deck, the CIL on schedule and the 5,200 koz reserve mined out — is worth Rp6,868, so the skew is positive on execution but not on gold alone.
Balance-sheet risk is not the reason to avoid the shares — shareholder facilities are undrawn and cash stays positive throughout. The valuation, not the mine, is the thesis.

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Merdeka Gold Resources with a **HOLD** and a twelve-month target of Rp4,971, -4.9% against the Rp5,225 share price. Our value is a life-of-mine discounted cash flow at the metals desk's through-cycle gold marker of US$4,300/oz, not at spot, and the target simply rolls that value forward one year at the cost of equity. The gap to the market is now small and it is not a disagreement about the quality of the mine: it is the difference between underwriting the marker and paying for a better gold price [S2, S11].

What the market is paying is visible in three places. The shares trade on 45.8x FY2026E earnings and 23.2x EV/EBITDA on our numbers — a multiple that already discounts the CIL ramp, which is why by FY2028E the same price is 7.2x earnings and 4.3x EV/EBITDA. Reverse-engineering the DCF, today's price requires a gold price of US$4,976/oz, about a sixth above our through-cycle marker and well above the US$4,075/oz spot print. That is a plausible gold call; it is simply not the one the house deck underwrites [S2, S11].

The asset itself is the best thing about the equity. Pani is the largest primary gold mine in Indonesia on a resources and reserves basis and ranks among the largest in Asia, with 5,200 koz of reserves that support 4,585 koz of planned output to the end of the plan, peak production of 545 koz and a strip ratio of 0.70 to one that is among the lowest of any large open pit [S11]. Costs are the second-best thing: cash cost excluding royalties and silver credits fell to US$778/oz in the third quarter of 2026, and the life-of-mine AISC including royalties is US$1,632/oz, a wide margin under the gold price we are modelling [S2, S11].

The problem is that the next two years are the expensive ones. The first CIL plant needs US$775.4m of capital in FY2027E alone, free cash flow is negative through FY2027E while the CIL is built, and leverage peaks at 2.3x on the pre-placement balance sheet before the CIL volumes arrive [S11, S2]. The company is bridging that with a placement of up to 1,470m new shares, for which it targets US$559.1m; at the Rp5,225 close the same shares support less than that, the exercise price is not yet set and approval is needed on 26 November 2026 [S7]. We carry the dilution and the proceeds the price rule supports symmetrically, so the placement is not itself a valuation argument — but a funding plan that depends on a shareholder vote is an execution risk the price does not reward.

Our scenarios put the bear case at Rp3,093, the base at Rp4,961 and the bull at Rp6,868, weighted 25%/50%/25%. The bull requires gold above the deck, the CIL on time and the rest of the reserve mined, so the upside is real but conditional; the weighted target of Rp4,971 is -4.9% from the price, which is a HOLD rather than a call in either direction. We would move to BUY on a share price that gives back the premium the placement has not yet diluted, or on the reserve conversion and CIL milestones landing together.

Gold doré is the unrefined bar that comes off a mine site before refining, and it is what Pani sells on to domestic buyers. Heap leaching dissolves gold from crushed ore stacked on lined pads and recovers it from solution; it is cheap to build and cheap to run but recovers a smaller share of the metal in the ore. Carbon-in-leach is a mill-based process that grinds the ore fine and leaches it in tanks with carbon present, which recovers more gold and costs far more to build. Moving from one to the other is the single largest capital decision a gold miner makes, and it is the pivot on which Pani's production profile turns.

PT Merdeka Gold Resources is an Indonesian gold miner whose only material asset is the Pani gold mine in Pohuwato Regency, Gorontalo Province, on the northern arm of Sulawesi [S11]. The company listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in September 2025 and added a secondary listing of Hong Kong depositary receipts on the Main Board of the Hong Kong exchange in 2026, at an offer price of 26.6 HKD per receipt [S3]. It reports in US dollars and sells in dollars, which matters for how we model both its revenue and much of its cost base [S2].

Pani is an open-pit operation that mines oxide and transitional ore and processes it through a heap leach circuit with an adsorption, desorption and recovery plant on site [S2]. The product is gold doré, sold as refined granules, with silver recovered as a by-product of the same doré; in the first nine months of 2026 the mine produced 84,611 oz of silver alongside its gold [S2]. There is one segment, one mine, one processing route and one product, so the revenue mix question that dominates most industrial coverage is simply answered: gold is effectively the whole company, and the silver credit is monetised as a deduction from unit cost rather than as a separate revenue line, which is how the company reports its cash cost [S2].

Ownership and group structure are straightforward but concentrated. PT Merdeka Copper Gold Tbk, the listed Indonesian copper and gold group, holds 64.8% of the shares and is the controlling shareholder; the free float is 25.7% of the register, with institutions and insiders accounting for 83.1% [S7, S6]. The company employs 631 people directly [S6]. Mining is carried out through operating subsidiaries under an IUP-OP production licence granted to PETS and valid to 2032, alongside a larger contract of work held by GSM that runs to 2049 and covers the bulk of the tenement area; the group describes the aggregate mining area as roughly fourteen and a half thousand hectares across the two titles [S11].

The commercial relationship that matters most today is the offtake. In February 2026 the mining subsidiary signed a gold sales and purchase agreement with PT Aneka Tambang, the state-owned diversified miner, for a two-year term and a total volume of up to 100 koz, selling refined gold granules domestically, with the first sale completed in March 2026 [S11]. Management states that sales under this agreement will represent a substantial proportion of revenue, so the company's realisations are anchored to a domestic buyer rather than to an international refining and trading chain [S11]. The agreement's finite volume means it will have to be renegotiated or replaced as output scales, which is a commercial negotiation we will be watching rather than a permanent feature of the business.

The growth plan is a two-step change in the nature of the asset. The first CIL plant is designed at 12.0 Mtpa with surge capacity that lifts throughput further, basic engineering is complete, all major long-lead equipment has been ordered and construction contractors have mobilised, with commissioning targeted for 2028 [S2, S12]. A second CIL plant of the same capacity is being studied on shared infrastructure; once both run, management guides combined CIL output capacity of 500 koz, on top of the heap leach, which is a step change rather than an incremental debottleneck [S2]. Exploration is funded but modest: an approved US$11.4m budget for 2027 covering a 50,000 m drill programme aimed at the Pani Deeps, the Pani Gap area and Kolokoa, where a maiden resource has already been added to the 7,000 koz Pani resource [S2, S3].

Measured against the domestic peer set, Pani is the leader rather than a challenger: the largest primary gold mine in Indonesia by resources and reserves, with an expected rank among the top two primary gold mines in Asia by production by 2030 [S11]. The competitive position rests on geology and geometry rather than on brand or switching costs — a large, low-strip, mountain-style orebody that can be mined with conventional equipment and processed with a simple flowsheet [S11]. That is a real advantage on cost, and it is also the reason the company is a price taker: nothing about the asset lets it influence the gold price it receives.

Indonesia's gold mining industry is dominated by a handful of large pits and by gold that comes as a by-product of copper. The country sits on the Pacific rim of fire, so its deposits are volcanic-hosted and often steeply mineralised, which is why the large mines tend to be high-grade but short-lived relative to the porphyry systems of South America. Most domestic production is sold into the local market or refined domestically, and the state miner has historically been the anchor buyer for gold produced by private miners.

Gold is not an industrial commodity with a demand curve that can be forecast from GDP. The metals desk's deck carries a through-cycle marker of US$4,300/oz that escalates with dollar inflation, against a spot print of US$4,075/oz at the time of writing — the marker sits above spot, which is unusual and reflects the desk's judgement that the real-yield and central-bank buying conditions of the past two years normalise rather than persist [S11]. Every valuation in this report is built on that marker. It is the single most important number in our work and it is not ours: it is the house view, and we defer to it rather than re-deriving a gold forecast, which is the discipline the commodity template is designed to enforce.

The revenue line that follows from it is mechanical: gold produced, multiplied by the benchmark, multiplied by a realisation ratio of 0.96 [S2]. That realisation ratio is not a marketing discount — it is the measured gap between the benchmark and the average price the company actually received, US$4,306/oz over the first nine months of 2026, measured against the same nine months of the metals desk's gold tape rather than against a forecast year [S2]. On that basis the ratio is in the mid-nineties, which is what we carry. It reflects the quotational period and the pricing mechanics of doré sales into the domestic market, and we hold it flat through the forecast because there is no evidence in the company's own disclosure that it improves with scale.

The industry structure that matters for Pani is the supply side. Indonesia holds the largest gold reserves in Asia, but most of those ounces sit in a small number of deposits, several of which are copper mines with gold credits rather than primary gold mines [S11]. That scarcity is what makes a standalone primary gold mine of Pani's size unusual, and it is the basis of management's claim to be among the largest primary gold mines in Asia on both resources and reserves [S11]. It is also why the domestic peer set is thin: the closest comparables are diversified miners with gold segments, not pure-play gold producers, which is a real constraint on relative valuation and the reason we do not weight a peer multiple in our target.

Regulation shapes the cash flow at three points, and all three are modelled explicitly. First, royalty: the gold royalty schedule is progressive with the gold price, and at the top bracket the rate is 16% of the price per ounce, which is what the company pays and what the reserve report assumes [S11]. Second, corporate income tax: Pani straddles two fiscal regimes, with the IUP-OP tenement paying 22% and the Contract of Work covering most of the tenement paying 35%, which the CPR blends pro rata to production into a year-by-year effective rate that runs at 22% in FY2026E, rises to 25% by FY2028E and 30% at the peak, then tapers over the tail [S11]. We carry that schedule rather than a flat statutory rate, because a flat rate would tax most of the orebody at the IUP rate it does not pay. Third, permitting: production requires an approved annual work plan and budget, which is why the company explicitly qualifies its 2027 guidance as subject to that approval [S2]. Each of these is a policy variable that can move against the equity without any change in the orebody, and each is captured in the model rather than left as a narrative risk.

The cost position is the company's clearest competitive advantage, and it is structural rather than cyclical. The orebody's average strip ratio is 0.70 to one over the life of the mine, which means very little waste has to be moved per tonne of ore; the reserve report's life-of-mine AISC including royalties is US$1,632/oz, and the first nine months of actual operation printed an AISC excluding royalties and silver credits of US$1,477/oz even at a fraction of design throughput, when unit costs should be at their worst [S11, S2]. Against a deck gold price of US$4,300/oz, that leaves a margin wide enough to absorb a great deal of cost inflation before the mine becomes marginal — which is precisely why the bear case in this report is about the gold price and the capital programme, not about the cost base.

Five-forces, briefly. Supplier power is moderate and rising during the build — heavy equipment rental, fuel and construction services are concentrated, the company's own top suppliers are service providers rather than single-source vendors, and the mining fleet has just been expanded to access higher-grade ore [S11, S2]. Buyer power is high in the short term because one domestic buyer takes a substantial share of output under a finite-volume agreement [S11], though that weakens as the market for a larger, refined product broadens. Threat of new entry is low in the sense that matters — a new primary gold mine of this size takes a decade to permit and build — but irrelevant to pricing, because the price is set in a global market. Substitution is not a factor for gold as an investment asset and only a slow one for jewellery. Rivalry within Indonesia is limited, with a small number of large producers and a long tail of small ones. The net of that is a narrow moat: the asset is genuinely hard to replicate, and the company has almost no pricing power with which to exploit it.

The external swing factors are gold and the rupiah. The company earns dollars, reports in dollars and pays most of its cost base in dollars, so a weaker rupiah lifts the rupiah share price roughly in proportion without touching the dollar cash flows; the sensitivity table in the valuation section confirms that this is a translation effect rather than operating leverage, and smaller than a comparable move in gold [S2]. Where the rupiah does bite on the operating side is through domestically sourced labour, fuel and services. We model the currency at the deck's path rather than taking a view.

Gold behaves less like a commodity than like a currency without a central bank. Its price responds to real interest rates, to the dollar, and to official-sector buying, which is why two economies with identical mine costs can be worth very different amounts per ounce depending on the cycle. Central banks have been net buyers for more than a decade, and investment demand through exchange-traded products can move the price far more in a quarter than mine supply can in a year. That is the sense in which gold miners are levered plays on an asset whose supply is slow and whose demand is sentiment-driven.

The historical record is thin by design, because the mine did not produce gold until 2026. Revenue to FY2025 was nominal, the company was loss-making with nominal EBITDA, and US$182.6m of capital was sunk into the Pani build [S4, S5]. Two adjustments matter for anyone reading the history. The data pack carries no mine depreciation for those loss-making years, while the audited accounts do charge a small amount of depreciation to cost of revenue; we have restated the historical depreciation line from the audited statements so that the pre-production loss is not flattered by an artificially clean cost of sales [S4, F40, F41]. And the balance sheet in the pack is stale, which we deal with below.

The 2026 ramp has been faster than the plan that underpins the reserve report. Production began in February 2026, reached 26,331 oz in the third quarter and 43,743 oz over the first nine months, with September alone at an annualised run rate of 130 koz and the first two weeks of October implying a rate a seventh higher again [S2]. Unit costs have fallen as throughput has risen: cash cost excluding royalties and silver credits was US$826/oz for the nine months but US$778/oz in the third quarter, and AISC on the same basis fell from US$1,477/oz to US$1,281/oz [S2]. That is the shape a heap leach should have — fixed cost spread over rising ounces — and it is the strongest operational evidence in the file that the flowsheet works.

Management nonetheless cut the year's guidance, narrowing it to a range whose floor is 85.0 koz while explicitly warning that timing may push some planned output into early 2027, and kept cash-cost and AISC guidance unchanged [S2]. We model the floor rather than the midpoint. We also model 170.0 koz in FY2027E, which is the smallest number consistent with both of the company's own statements that 2027 output will be well above its earlier 150 koz estimate and that combined heap leach output across 2026 and 2027 will exceed 250 koz [S2]. From FY2028E we follow the reserve report's annual production schedule, which peaks at 545 koz in 2031 and tails off to the end of the plan [S11]. No volume is credited for the second CIL plant, because it has no published timetable or capital estimate — it is an option, described in the risk section, not a forecast.

One timing feature of the 2026 numbers needs to be stated plainly. Reported gold sales lag production badly: 15,635 oz sold against 43,743 oz produced over the first nine months, because doré granules are held for sale and part of that inventory is now effectively pre-sold through the US$100.0m prepayment facility, which settles in quarterly instalments through 2027 [S2]. Our template books revenue on produced ounces, so the FY2026E revenue line of US$366.7m is a production-economics figure that runs ahead of the shipment pattern; the difference is inventory value that shows up in FY2027E cash flow rather than value that disappears. We treat it as a timing item, and we flag it because a reader comparing our FY2026E revenue with the reported 2026 accounts will otherwise think we are wrong.

On that basis the forecast is a ramp followed by a step change. Our base case produces US$366.7m of revenue and US$203.1m of EBITDA at a 55.4% margin in FY2026E; US$701.8m and US$413.6m in FY2027E as heap leach throughput reaches the reserve report's second-year rate; and US$1,651.2m and US$1,086.3m once the first CIL plant is commissioned, with revenue rising to US$1,828.7m the following year [S11, S2]. Net profit attributable to shareholders runs from US$102.1m in FY2026E to US$646.3m in FY2028E.

The cost build follows the reserve report's life-of-mine cost and depreciation tables rather than a top-down margin assumption, because a mine plan is a better forecast of unit cost than a spreadsheet ratio [S11]. Unit cash cost starts at US$826, the nine-month actual, falls to US$581 as CIL throughput spreads fixed mining and administrative cost over far more ounces, and then escalates with the deck's long-run dollar inflation so that the modelled margin does not widen artificially over the tail [S2, S11]. Royalty is charged at 16% of revenue, and it is the difference between the pre-royalty cash cost in the reserve report and the US$1,632/oz life-of-mine AISC we carry [S11]. Depreciation and expansion capital are taken from the same tables, which is why depreciation steps up with the CIL and capex is front-loaded into the build years [S11].

Capital spending is the reason the next two years look weak. We carry US$299.2m of capex in FY2026E and US$775.4m in FY2027E, the great majority of it the first CIL plant together with the associated tailings and infrastructure, falling to US$164.0m once commissioning is done [S11]. Free cash flow is therefore negative in both build years — US$299.2m of capex against US$203.1m of EBITDA in FY2026E, and considerably worse in FY2027E — before turning to US$617.1m and US$847.7m as the CIL ounces arrive [S11].

The balance sheet has to be read from the third-quarter report rather than from the pack. At 30 September 2026 cash, net of restricted balances, was US$125.0m against US$674.0m of debt: a finance lease of US$74.0m, the ING prepayment of US$100.0m, the US$350.0m Pani revolving facility drawn in full and the US$150.0m EMAS facility also drawn [S2]. The pack's debt figure is the June balance and predates both the prepayment received in late September and the facility drawdown, so we anchor the forecast to the September figure and roll the year-end debt to it [S2]. Behind that sits a set of shareholder facilities from PT Merdeka Copper Gold, none of them drawn, which is a genuine liquidity backstop rather than a funding plan [S2].

Leverage peaks at 2.3x net debt to EBITDA in FY2026E and 2.3x in FY2027E, then falls to 0.3x in FY2028E as the CIL cash arrives [S11]. Those ratios are measured before the placement, because the model's net debt is the cumulative cash deficit of the mine plan and is neutral to how that deficit is financed; the placement is what lowers it in practice, and the same 1,470m shares are the reason the figure is a peak rather than a permanent condition. The placement targets US$559.1m for working capital and debt reduction, with the balance available for development and capital spending, and is conditional on shareholder approval at the meeting on 26 November 2026 [S7]. We treat the dilution and the proceeds the price rule supports as a wash in valuation and put the proceeds in the bridge so the equity is not penalised twice; the placement is nonetheless a real risk, because a vote that fails leaves the FY2027E funding gap to be met with more debt at a floating rate.

Capital allocation is conservative on the evidence available. The dividend policy allows a distribution only when the company has positive retained earnings, and interim dividends are permitted within statutory limits, but nothing has been paid and we assume nothing is paid [S6]. The consequence in the model is that no dividend is distributed at any point in the plan and the cash balance simply accumulates [S6]. That is a conservatism on our side rather than a prediction — a company that reaches the end of a mine life with that much cash and no dividend in operation would be an obvious candidate for a distribution or a reinvestment decision, and the market will price the probability of both long before 2040.

Earnings quality: four flags, all of which we have resolved rather than left hanging. The sales-to-production gap is the largest and is a timing effect created by doré inventory and the prepayment structure [S2]. The historical depreciation line was empty in the pack and has been restated from the audited statements [S4]. The per-ounce royalty metric in the operating table — US$70.0/oz per ounce sold for the nine months, which the company reports alongside its cash cost — looks far below the 16% rate applied to revenue, and we reconciled it: the per-ounce figure is computed on produced ounces while the royalty is charged on revenue from sold ounces, and both the reserve report and the income statement confirm the rate we model [S2, S11]. Finally, the auditor's opinion on the FY2025 accounts is unqualified, from a firm in the BDO network, and there is no qualification, emphasis or restatement in the file that would change our view of the reported numbers [S4].

The primary method is a life-of-mine discounted cash flow, and the reason is structural rather than a preference. Pani is a finite orebody with a published reserve, a published annual production schedule and a published cost and capital profile, so the cash flows can be modelled from the company's own mine plan rather than from a growth assumption [S11]. We discount free cash flow to the firm over the full plan to FY2040E, take no terminal value beyond it, and value the equity as enterprise value less net debt, less minorities, plus investments and the placement bridge [S11]. The method carries no terminal growth assumption, because the mine physically ends; the 2.0% growth in the model is used only to escalate the gold benchmark and the cost base, not to create a perpetuity.

The cost of capital is built bottom-up and lands at 11.41%. The dollar risk-free rate is 4.86%, the mature-market equity risk premium 4.23% and the Indonesia country risk premium 2.46%; the unlevered beta of 1.00 is the industry default for precious and base metals in this model rather than a regression on the company's own, because there is not enough trading history to estimate one — the shares listed only in late 2025 [S11]. Relevered at the company's own debt-to-equity ratio of 0.16, that gives a cost of equity of 12.38%. Debt costs 6.86% pre-tax, consistent with a floating-rate facility book priced off dollar rates plus a margin, and the weights are 86.3% equity and 13.7% debt at market values — the equity weight dominates because the market capitalisation is large relative to net debt [S2].

The discounted cash flow produces an enterprise value of US$4,075.7m and a value per share of Rp4,415. Almost all of that value is created after FY2028E, which is the defining feature of the investment case: the two years of negative free cash flow at the front of the plan are the price of admission to a decade of strong cash generation, and the market is paying for the later years now [S11]. The valuation date is 30 September 2026 for the balance sheet and 8 November 2026 for discounting; the one structural caveat is that the engine's FY2026E stub is counted from the pack's 30 June balance-sheet date while the net debt is the 30 September restatement, so a quarter of cash flow is counted in both — we have not been able to move the stub date without editing the data pack, and the effect is a small understatement of value, well inside the scenario range and not enough to change the rating.

The bridge from enterprise value to equity is net debt at the valuation date, plus the placement proceeds the price rule supports at the current close, net of the dilution they cause [S7]. We do not carry the company's headline US$559.1m target: [S7] states the exercise price is unset and must be at least nine-tenths of the trailing average closing price over the preceding month of trading days, and at the Rp5,225 close the maximum on 1,470m new shares is below that target, so the bridge carries the achievable amount and the FY2027 debt draw is set to the residual rather than to the full fallback. That is why our per-share value is below the enterprise value divided by the current share count.

The multiple-based cross-checks are shown for reference and carry no weight in the target, for reasons we think are defensible. A price-to-book cross-check is meaningless while the book value is being rebuilt from a pre-production base — the shares trade on 9.7x book today and 3.5x on our FY2028E book, and the ratio is falling because the denominator is growing, not because the market is repricing the asset. An EV/EBITDA cross-check needs a peer group of comparable gold producers, and there is no clean listed set: the domestic comparables are diversified miners whose EBITDA comes mostly from copper or nickel, and the international pure-play gold producers trade on cycle positions and jurisdictions that are not comparable to a single Indonesian heap leach turning into a CIL operation [S11]. Rather than import a multiple we cannot defend, we let the cash flow do the work and treat the multiples as a sanity check on the shape of the earnings path — and the shape is sensible: the multiple compresses from 45.8x to 7.2x earnings as the CIL volumes arrive.

The sensitivity grid makes the hierarchy of value drivers explicit. Gold is the dominant operating driver: a move of a tenth in the benchmark moves the target by roughly three times as much as a ten-percent change in volume, and no combination of volume and unit-cost outcomes in the second grid spans more than about a fifth of value. That is not a modelling artefact, it is the economics of a high-margin gold producer — with unit cash cost near US$826 and a benchmark near US$4,300/oz, most of the revenue line is operating leverage, and a tenth off the price takes a large bite out of the margin. The rupiah sits between the two: because the valuation is struck in dollars and translated into the share price, a weaker rupiah lifts the rupiah target roughly in proportion, which is a translation effect rather than a source of edge. The practical implication is that the case for the shares is a case about gold, and it should be argued that way.

Reverse-engineering the price gives the same answer from the other direction. Holding volumes, costs and the discount rate at our base case, today's Rp5,225 requires a gold price of US$4,976/oz to earn the cost of equity [S11]. Compare that with the through-cycle marker of US$4,300/oz and the spot print of US$4,075/oz: the market is not pricing spot, and it is not pricing our marker either, but something about a sixth above it. Our sensitivity grid agrees — the price is cleared once the benchmark is around a sixth above the deck. An investor buying the shares here is therefore making a modestly bullish gold call, and if that is the intention the equity is a reasonable vehicle for it; it is not a call we can underwrite at this level, and the price is close enough to our value that the rating is HOLD rather than a directional call.

The honest caveats on the valuation are four. The first is that the DCF has no terminal value, so the value is the discounted sum of a plan that ends with a small tail — a mine life extension from Kolokoa or the Pani Deeps exploration would add value that is not in the base case, and the 5,200 koz reserve includes ounces the plan does not mine [S2, S6]. We credit those ounces in the bull case, not the base, because the CIL reserve is capped by tailings capacity of 143 Mt and the heap leach by 62.0 Mt of pad capacity, so converting the extra reserve needs permitting and more storage before it can be scheduled [S6]. The second is that a 2028 CIL start is assumed without contingency: the capital is spread over FY2026E and FY2027E, and a year's delay would cut the value by roughly the cash flow of the deferred year, which the sensitivity grid does not capture — the bear case carries both a slip in volume and a capital overrun for that reason. The third is that the realisation ratio of 0.96 is held flat even though a second domestic buyer or a change in the pricing mechanism could move it; a percentage point of realisation is worth more than most of the operational variables in the grid. The fourth is the placement: its size, price and approval are all still open, and the bridge carries what today's price supports rather than the company's target.

Gold price is the first risk and by a distance the largest. Our base case uses a through-cycle marker of US$4,300/oz while spot is US$4,075/oz, so the marker is above the market — a position that would be wrong if real yields stay high or if official-sector demand fades [S11]. The bear case takes the benchmark well below the marker, and the valuation consequence is severe because the mine has no other way to defend its margin. Likelihood: medium over a twelve-month horizon. Impact: high. The mitigation is not in the company's hands; it is in the sizing of the position.

Execution of the CIL build is the second. The company has ordered its long-lead equipment and mobilised contractors, and basic engineering is complete, but the same management team has just cut its own production guidance for the year and flagged slippage into 2027 [S2]. That is a track record worth weighing: a heap leach ramp that slipped is not the same as a process plant build, but it is evidence that the timetable is optimistic. The capital is US$775.4m in FY2027E, so a year's delay defers the start of the strong cash years without reducing the spend, and a capital overrun of the kind common on first-of-a-kind process plants would land on a balance sheet that is already funding a negative free cash flow [S11]. The bear case therefore carries both: volume light as the plant slips and capital over budget. It would leave the leverage peak at 2.3x for longer than the plan assumes. Likelihood: medium. Impact: high.

Funding and dilution are the third. The placement of up to 1,470m new shares, for which the company targets US$559.1m, needs shareholder approval on 26 November 2026; the exercise price is not yet set and is floored at nine-tenths of the trailing average closing price over the preceding month of trading days, so at today's price it raises less than the target [S7]. A rejection would leave a company with negative free cash flow and a leverage peak to fund from debt markets at a floating rate, and would restore the full fallback debt draw in our model. Approval dilutes existing holders by 9.98%; rejection risks a harder funding outcome. Our model treats the two symmetrically, but the market may not, and a failed vote would be a genuine adverse event rather than a wash. Likelihood: low. Impact: material.

Permitting and the licence horizon are the fourth, and they are underappreciated. The production licence held by the mining subsidiary expires in 2032, eight years before the end of the modelled plan, and the company notes that applications for certain construction and operating permits are still in progress [S11]. The larger contract of work covering most of the tenement runs to 2049, which is the argument for why this is manageable, but a renewal process that runs late, or a change in the royalty or tax regime as part of it, would hit a valuation that assumes both are stable [S11]. Annual work-plan approval is a further, recurring gate that the company itself flags as a condition on its 2027 guidance [S2]. Likelihood: low in the near term. Impact: high if it materialises.

Reserve conversion and tailings capacity are the fifth. The reserve is estimated at a gold price of US$2,300/oz, far below the price the mine will sell at, which is reassuring on the reserve itself but also means the reserve is a floor rather than a ceiling on what the orebody contains [S6]. The CIL reserve is capped by tailings storage capacity of 143 Mt across the existing facility and the filtered plant, and the heap leach reserve by 62.0 Mt of pad capacity [S6]. Mine-life extension therefore depends on permitting and building more storage, not just on drilling; the Kolokoa and Pani Deeps results may add ounces that cannot be converted into reserves without it [S2, S6]. Likelihood: medium over the plan. Impact: medium.

Single-asset and single-jurisdiction concentration is the sixth, and it is structural rather than a forecast. One mine, one processing route, one product, one province, and one customer taking a substantial share of output [S11]. Any of a dozen operational events — a slope failure, a leach pad problem, a tailings issue, a fire — is a company-wide event rather than a segment event. The company carries insurance and posts reclamation collateral, but no insurance covers the equity multiple [S6]. Likelihood: low per event. Impact: high.

Governance and related-party risk is the seventh. A 64.8% controlling shareholder, a free float of 25.7%, and a funding structure in which the controlling group is also the provider of undrawn standby facilities creates the conditions in which minority interests depend on the controller's choices [S7, S2]. We see no evidence of abuse in the file and the related-party balances we can see are disclosed in detail, but a controlled company raising equity at a discount while its parent provides standby debt is a structure that deserves a governance discount rather than the benefit of the doubt.

Cost inflation and currency are the eighth and smallest. The mine earns dollars and pays most of its cost in dollars, so the rupiah is a translation effect rather than an operating one, and unit costs have so far come in at or below plan [S2, S11]. Domestic labour, fuel and contractor rates are the real exposures, and they are captured in the escalation we apply from FY2030E onwards rather than assumed away.

The scenarios are built on the same four drivers in mirrored pairs, with one sourced asymmetry. The bear case puts gold well below the through-cycle marker, assumes the CIL slips into 2029 with the ramp repeating the 2026 pattern of guidance cuts, and adds a cost shock and a capital overrun; it produces a value of Rp3,093, 25% probability. The base case is the plan as published, at the through-cycle marker, worth Rp4,961 at 50%. The bull case has gold and costs the mirror of the bear's, the CIL on schedule, and the 5,200 koz reserve mined rather than the 4,585 koz the plan schedules — the one asymmetry, sourced from the reserve statement rather than assumed — worth Rp6,868 at 25%. The second CIL plant is not added separately even in the bull: it has no published capital estimate or timetable, and its value is the extra throughput already credited, so counting both would double-count the same ounces [S2]. The probability-weighted target of Rp4,971 is -4.9% against the share price, which is why the rating is HOLD: the distribution is wide, the bull case is worth a third more than the price, and the base case sits a little below it.

The signposts that would change our mind, in order of how quickly they could arrive: a gold benchmark that holds above the level implied by the current price for a full quarter rather than a week; the 26 November meeting approving the placement and the company actually applying the proceeds to debt; the 2027 work-plan approval carrying an output range at or above our number rather than a restatement of the old one; and the CIL plant reaching mechanical completion inside the 2028 window with capital in line. Any two of those together would move us to BUY even without a change in the gold price, because they would remove the execution risk that keeps our target close to the price.

Ownership is concentrated but compliant. PT Merdeka Copper Gold holds 64.8% of the shares and is the controlling shareholder; the public free float is 25.7%, comfortably above the exchange's minimum, and insiders and institutions together account for 83.1% of the register [S7, S6]. EMAS does not appear on the house registry of conglomerate-controlled issuers, so the conglomerate lens does not apply here, and there is no index-deletion or enforcement history attached to the name in our records. The concentration is nonetheless real: a holder of that size can carry an ordinary resolution, which is why the placement is being put to shareholders rather than decided by the board.

The board has been stable but not long-tenured. Boyke Poerbaya Abidin is President Director, and Santoso Kartono was appointed President Commissioner at an extraordinary meeting in December 2025, replacing the previous incumbent [S6]. The company discloses concurrent positions for directors and commissioners, which is standard practice for an Indonesian issuer of this size and is a point to monitor rather than a red flag [S6]. The audit opinion on the FY2025 accounts is unqualified and comes from a firm in the BDO network, with no restatement or qualification in the file [S4].

Related-party dealing is the area to watch, and the visible balances are transparent. The controlling shareholder has extended three standby facilities, all undrawn at 30 September 2026, and the company discloses the terms of each [S2]. The supply chain runs through a small number of contractors for equipment rental, fuel and construction services, which is normal for a mine of this age but concentrates procurement exposure in a handful of counterparties [S11]. We have no evidence that any of those arrangements is on terms worse than arm's length, and the company's disclosure of them is more detailed than most in the sector.

The capital-markets record is active, and minority holders should price that. The company listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in 2025, completed a secondary listing of depositary receipts in Hong Kong in 2026 at 26.6 HKD per receipt, and is now proposing a placement of 1,470m new shares worth US$559.1m [S3, S7]. It also completed a capital reduction that cancelled a large block of shares before the listing, which is why the 14,731m listed shares differ from the pre-reduction count [S6]. None of that is improper; all of it is the behaviour of a company that uses its equity currency repeatedly, and repeated issuance below our estimate of value is precisely how minority holders lose money in a controlled company.

The dividend record is empty and the policy is cautious. Distributions require positive retained earnings and shareholder approval, interim dividends are permitted within statutory limits, and nothing has been paid [S6]. We model no dividend, which is the conservative choice for a company in a build phase, but it leaves the equity with no cash return for the foreseeable future and makes the total return entirely a function of the share price.

Environmental exposure is concentrated in two places: tailings and water. The mine's CIL reserve is limited by tailings storage capacity — 143 Mt across the existing facility and a filtered tailings plant, with the filtered facility the reason the company can claim dry-stacked storage for part of the stream [S6]. Tailings dam failures are the existential risk in this industry, and the mitigations that matter are design, monitoring and disclosure, none of which we can audit from outside; the company discloses its storage arrangements at a level that is better than average but not best-in-class. Water management, acid rock drainage from the waste dumps and the post-closure rehabilitation obligation are the other long-dated liabilities, and the company posts reclamation collateral as required [S6]. On emissions, the company has a net-zero target for 2060 at group level and cites hydroelectric power and carbon-reduction measures among its initiatives, which is a policy statement rather than a plan with capital attached [S6].

Social and labour exposure is domestic and local. The mine employs 631 people directly and runs community development programmes designed around local needs, in a province where mining is one of the few large formal employers [S6]. That is a source of licence to operate and a source of cost pressure at the same time — local content expectations tend to rise with the size of the operation, and the CIL build will raise both. There is no strike, blockade or community dispute in the disclosure record, which is a positive given the asset's history.

The first dated catalyst is the shareholders' meeting on 26 November 2026, at which approval is sought for the placement of up to 1,470m new shares and its use for working capital and debt reduction [S7]. Approval removes the funding overhang and allows the proceeds to be applied to the facilities; rejection forces a different funding path in a year when free cash flow is negative. We will read the outcome as a signal about how the controlling shareholder intends to treat the minority in future capital raisings, not just as a funding event.

The second is the FY2026 reporting cycle, beginning with the fourth-quarter activities report and the audited results. Three things matter there: whether reported sales close the gap to production, which would confirm the inventory timing rather than a demand problem [S2]; whether the full-year cash cost and AISC land inside the guidance ranges the company has kept unchanged [S2]; and whether the reserve and resource statement is updated for the Kolokoa maiden resource and the Pani Deeps drilling [S3].

The third is the 2027 work plan and budget approval, which the company itself names as the condition on its 2027 output guidance [S2]. The number to watch is not the approval itself but the range that accompanies it: a range anchored above our 170.0 koz would confirm that the 2026 slippage is genuinely timing, while a range that restates the old estimate would tell us the ramp is slower than the mine plan.

The fourth is the CIL build, which is a two-year monitoring exercise rather than a single event. The milestones are the award of the remaining procurement packages, which management expects by the end of 2026 [S2]; the completion of the starter dam embankment through 2027 [S2]; and mechanical completion and commissioning in the 2028 window [S2]. Slippage on any of those is the most direct route to the bear case, and it is observable quarters before it shows up in the accounts.

The operating measures we will track between updates are the monthly gold pour and the annualised run rate it implies, since that is the leading indicator of whether guidance is met [S2]; the cash cost and AISC per ounce excluding royalties and silver credits, which is the company's own measure and the one comparable with its guidance [S2]; the strip ratio and ore tonnes mined, because the third quarter's ore was taken at a higher grade than the mining plan ahead of schedule, which flatters near-term cost and cannot persist [S2]; the balance of doré inventory and the settlement schedule of the prepayment facility, both of which drive the gap between production and cash [S2]; and net debt against the leverage path, where the peak at 2.3x is the number that determines whether the funding plan is adequate [S11].

Finally, the two strategic options we do not model are worth monitoring because they could change the value materially in either direction. The second CIL plant would roughly double processing capacity on shared infrastructure, but it has no published capital estimate or timetable, so it is an option whose value we cannot size [S2]. And the exploration programme at the Pani Deeps, the Pani Gap area and Kolokoa could extend a mine life that currently ends in 2040, but any extension needs tailings capacity as well as ounces, and the storage limit of 143 Mt is the binding constraint on converting those ounces into reserves [S2, S6].

bear.narrative: Gold mean-reverts below the deck: the bear takes the benchmark 15% under the 4,300/oz through-cycle marker as real yields stay high and central-bank buying slows, and volume comes in 5% light because the 2028 CIL commissioning slips into 2029 and the ramp repeats the 2026 pattern of guidance cuts. Costs run 5% above the base path and the CIL build 10% over budget, so the cash-cost anchor is re-shocked rather than held. The royalty stays at 16% and the reserve base is unchanged; the bear is a price, timing and execution case, not an asset-integrity case.

bull.narrative: Gold holds above the deck: fiscal deficits and continued official-sector demand keep the benchmark 15% over the 4,300/oz marker, and Pani delivers more than its published plan. The CIL plant reaches nameplate in 2028, the 20% surge capacity is used, and the 615 koz of stated reserve that sits outside the 4,585 koz plan is mined on the same infrastructure - about 13% more ounces over the life than the base case carries. Unit costs run 5% below base as throughput spreads the fixed base, and the build comes in 10% under budget. The second CIL plant is not added separately: it has no published capital estimate or timetable, and its value is the extra throughput already credited here, so adding both would double-count it.

assumptions.label: Gold produced (koz)
assumptions.basis: The production path is the company's own mine plan, not a build-up. FY2026E 85 koz is the LOWER bound of the guidance narrowed on 2 November 2026 to 85-100 koz, chosen because 9M actual output was 43,743 oz and the company flags timing slippage into 2027 [F1, F3]; the September exit rate was ~130 koz annualised [F38] and October ran at ~149 koz annualised, so 85 is the conservative end of what the company itself still guides. FY2027E 170 koz is the smallest round number consistent with both of the company's own 2027 statements: output "well above" its earlier 150 koz estimate [F4] and combined heap leach output for 2026 and 2027 above 250 koz [F45], which with 85 koz in 2026 requires MORE than 165 koz. The CPR's 159 koz for 2027 [F18] is therefore treated as the floor of the 2027 range, not the centre. FY2028E-FY2040E are the CPR's annual gold-produced series (400/443/505/545/ 443/295/299/301/300/322/311/92/63 koz), which reflects the first CIL plant commissioned in 2028 (12 Mtpa, 20% surge to 14.4 Mtpa) and peak output of 545 koz in 2031 [S2 p.1, S11, F17, F18]. No volume is added for the second CIL plant announced as a feasibility update, because it has no published timetable or capex [S2 p.1]; the option is described in §5, not modelled.

assumptions.label: Realised gold price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: 0.96 of the benchmark in every year. Tested on the actual same-period benchmark, not on a forecast year: the metals deck carries the 2026 quarterly tape (Q1 4,876, Q2 4,512, Q3 4,268 USD/oz), a 9M 2026 average of US$4,552/oz, so the 9M ASP of US$4,306/oz [F6] is a realisation of 0.946, and the 3Q ASP of US$4,201/oz against the 3Q benchmark of 4,268 is 0.984. 0.96 sits inside that measured range (0.95-0.98) and at the peer norm, so it is not a haircut; it is the mid-point of the two actual measures. The gap is a doré discount (refining and treatment deductions on top of the CPR's 99.5% payable factor, which measures payable metal rather than price realisation) rather than a hedged book: EMAS sells at spot under its agreement with Antam and holds no hedge programme in the record. 0.96 is held flat because the discount is contractual, not cyclical; the bull/bear cases move the benchmark, not the ratio. Q3's realised ASP is also the cross-check on the revenue line: 8,680 oz sold at US$4,201 [F11, F6] reproduces the reported quarterly revenue.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap
assumptions.basis: No price cap or domestic-market obligation applies to gold doré; all output is sold at spot [S2 p.12].

assumptions.label: Cost-intensity factor (1.0 = cash cost per ounce is already unitised)
assumptions.basis: 1.0 in every year. The template multiplies strip_ratio by cost_per_bcm to get unit cash cost; the CPR already reports operating costs per ounce for a mine whose life-of-mine strip ratio is 0.7:1 [F16], so the physical stripping intensity is embedded in the per-ounce cost and a second multiplier would double-count it. The 0.7:1 average is disclosed in §2 as the reason the cost curve sits in the lowest quartile, not as a separate cost driver.

assumptions.label: Cash cost per ounce, net of silver credit, excluding royalty and G&A (USD/oz)
assumptions.basis: Built from two anchored segments. FY2026E 826 and FY2027E 778 are the company's own cash-cost measure (excluding royalties and silver credits) at the last actual and the quarter before it: 9M 2026 US$826/oz and 3Q 2026 US$778/oz [F7, F8]. 2027 holds the 3Q run-rate in real terms rather than the CPR's US$674/oz, because the CPR's 2026-27 cost assumes 20.4 Mt mined and a much larger mining rate than the 1.7 Mt actually mined in 3Q 2026 [F39]; holding the last actual is the most-likely rule. FY2028E-FY2040E come from the CPR's Table 15-5: total mine, heap-leach, CIL and tailings operating cost divided by gold produced [S11, F22], less the silver credit per gold ounce implied by the CPR's silver revenue and price [S11], which is how the company defines its own cash cost. The step down in 2028 (US$581/oz) is the first CIL plant lifting throughput from 165 to 400 koz on largely fixed mining and G&A, and the step up in 2039-40 is the low-volume tail (92 and 63 koz). From FY2030E the CPR's real-terms values are grown at the macro deck's 2.0% long-run USD inflation, matching the gold benchmark's own escalation (the deck carries 4,300/oz growing 2% a year from 2030), so the modelled margin does not widen artificially over the tail.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: Kept at the engine default 0.3. The CPR puts diesel at 2-4% of life-of-mine AISC [S11], so fuel is a minor input and the brent line in the macro deck is flat at 84 USD/bbl; a lower share would not move the valuation.

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit
assumptions.basis: Zero: every cash cost line the company reports (mining, heap-leach and CIL processing, tailings, site G&A, and the silver credit) is already inside cost_per_bcm and opex_pct [S2 Table 1, S11 Table 15-5], so a second per-ounce bucket would double-count.

assumptions.label: Gold royalty rate
assumptions.basis: 0.16 flat. The Indonesian gold royalty is progressive on the HMA (7% below US$1,800/oz, rising to 16% at or above US$3,000/oz) [S11, F19], and the reviewed gold deck is above that top threshold in every forecast year (FY2026E 4,493.75, FY2027E-lt 4,300 USD/oz), so the schedule yields 16% throughout. The actual P&L confirms it: 1H 2026 royalties were US$5.0m on revenue of US$30.9m (16.2%) and the CPR's own cash flow applies 16% to gold revenue [S3 p.8, S11]. Silver carries a separate 5% royalty; it is netted inside the silver credit rather than modelled as a second revenue line.

assumptions.label: Other revenue (silver is carried as a cost credit, not a revenue line)
assumptions.basis: Zero. Silver production of 84,611 oz in 9M 2026 [F5] is monetised through the silver credit in cost_per_bcm, matching the company's own cash-cost definition [S2 Table 1]; the 9M credit was US$70/oz of gold and the 3Q credit US$116/oz [F12, F13]. Adding silver revenue as well would double-count it.

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: Inert - other_revenue is zero in every year.

assumptions.label: D&A per ounce (USD/oz)
assumptions.basis: The CPR's annual depreciation and amortisation divided by gold produced: US$53.8m in 2026, 106.2m in 2027, then 169.2/162.9/159.3m [S11, F23]. 2026 is spread over the model's 85 koz (US$633/oz) rather than the CPR's 108 koz, because the charge is on the asset base, not the volume. The 2040 step in the CPR (US$434.8m) is the mine-closure provision unwinding; that is normalised to US$300/oz and the cash closure cost is carried in capex_unit instead, so the tail is not charged twice. From FY2030E the CPR's real-terms values are grown at the macro deck's 2.0% long-run USD inflation, matching the gold benchmark's own escalation (the deck carries 4,300/oz growing 2% a year from 2030), so the modelled margin does not widen artificially over the tail.

assumptions.label: Total capex per ounce, expansion plus sustaining plus closure (USD/oz)
assumptions.basis: CPR Table 15-5 expansion capital plus sustaining capital plus mine closure, divided by gold produced [S11, F24]. The shape is the investment story: US$299m in 2026 and US$725m in 2027 are the CIL build (basic engineering complete, long-lead equipment ordered, commissioning targeted 2028) [S2 p.1], then capex falls to US$164m in 2028 and to sustaining levels of roughly US$20m a year [S11]. The 2039 and 2040 lines add the CPR's US$33m and US$17m of mine closure cash, which is why the tail unit capex rises. 2026 is divided by the model's 85 koz rather than the CPR's 108 koz because the spend is a project budget, not a per-ounce rate (US$306m plan). From FY2030E the CPR's real-terms values are grown at the macro deck's 2.0% long-run USD inflation, matching the gold benchmark's own escalation (the deck carries 4,300/oz growing 2% a year from 2030), so the modelled margin does not widen artificially over the tail.

assumptions.label: Other capex
assumptions.basis: Zero - all expansion and sustaining spend is in capex_unit, and the 2027 exploration budget of US$11.4m [F37] is expensed through opex_pct.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: 8% of revenue. The engine default (-100%) is a pre-production artefact of the 2022-25 revenue base, which was equipment rental rather than doré sales. The CPR's own working-capital line is the better guide: US$75.7m in 2027 on revenue of US$888m is 8.5%, falling as inventory and payables settle [S11 Table 15-5]. 8% applies that ratio to the model's revenue line.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate (IUP/CoW blend)
assumptions.basis: The CPR's own year-by-year effective rate, which blends PETS' IUP rate of 22% with GSM's Contract of Work rate of 35% pro rata to mining production in each year [S11 p.216, p.638]. Pani straddles both tenements, so the blended rate rises from 22% in 2026-27 to 25-30% from 2028 as CoW output grows, peaking at 30% in 2032 before tapering to 25% in 2040 [S11 Table 15-5, p.206]. The CPR cash-flow model's income-tax row is 22/22/25/26/26/26/30/27/29/28/28/26/28/29/25% for 2026-40, and its tax-payable line reconciles to those rates (e.g. 2028 taxable income US$1,489.5m x 25% = US$369.2m). The FY2025 effective rate in the data pack (13.1%) is meaningless: the company was pre-production and loss-making, so it reflects deferred-tax movements rather than a cash rate. A flat 22% is the IUP rate only and understates tax on the CoW production; no tax holiday or investment allowance appears in the record.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt
assumptions.basis: 6.86%, the same rate the cost-of-capital block uses: the macro deck's dollar risk-free rate of 4.859% plus a 2.00% facility margin on the drawn book (Pani RCF, EMAS RCF, ING gold prepayment), which is how the cost of debt is built for the WACC [S2 p.12]. FY2025 finance expense of US$13.69m on average debt of US$245m was 5.6% on a smaller, partly pre-drawal balance, so the forward rate is the facility build rather than the historical average.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 3.0% on USD cash and short-term deposits, against a 6.0% debt cost, consistent with the small positive carry the 9M 2026 accounts show on a net-debt position.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing (external funding of the CIL build, then repayment)
assumptions.basis: FY2026E US$384.4m is a balance-sheet alignment, not a forecast drawdown: the engine rolls the forecast balance sheet forward from the FY2025 audited position (debt US$289.6m) while the valuation anchors on the 30 September 2026 report (debt US$674m), so the difference is booked here to keep the closing debt in line with what the company had actually drawn - the Pani RCF, the EMAS RCF and the ING gold prepayment [S2 p.12]. FY2027E US$26m is the residual debt draw once the placement is assumed to land: the unlevered cash flow is deeply negative in 2027 (CIL capex of US$725m against US$656m of revenue) and the CPR shows the same thing - a projected negative cash flow of US$304.2m for 2027, which the company says it will fund with new bank loans or capital-market issuance [S11 p.205]. The placement raises US$424.0m at the current Rp5,225 close (1.47bn shares x Rp5,225 / 18,103), which covers most of the US$450m need; only the shortfall is drawn here, so the leverage path and the valuation use the SAME funding case instead of carrying the equity and the fallback debt at once [S7, F33]. If the placement is voted down at the 26 November RUPS the draw reverts to US$450m, which is the downside case in the report. The draws are repaid from 2028-29 free cash flow (US$350m and US$100m), leaving debt near its opening level by 2030.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero - no recurring non-operating line appears in the record; the FY2025 and 1H 2026 "other expenses" are one-off listing and financing costs already inside the historical pack.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Zero - non-controlling interests on the balance sheet are US$0.04m against US$361.5m of equity, and the 1H 2026 net loss carries no minority portion [S3 p.8].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero in every year. EMAS has no dividend policy in the record: it has never paid a dividend (dps_ttm 0), it is funding a US$1.4bn CIL build, and the CPR's cash flow contains no dividend line [S11, S2]. The dividend-capacity section of the report shows what the free cash flow would support, without assuming it is paid.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: +9.98% in FY2026E for the private placement of up to 1.47 billion new shares on a base of 14,731,366,060 [F33, F32], i.e. 16,201,366,060 shares pro forma. This line drives the displayed share count and EPS only; the per-share valuation uses the pro-forma count carried in the bs_shares fact [F31], so the dilution is inside the denominator of every per-share method.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Inert - the valuation uses dcf_life, a life-of-asset DCF with no terminal value, because the mine plan ends in 2040 [S11, F17].

assumptions.label: Cash G&A and exploration / revenue
assumptions.basis: The CPR's G&A line divided by the model's revenue: US$26.0m in 2026 (7.1% of the model's US$367m revenue), 32.0m in 2027 (4.9%), 55.4m in 2028 (3.4%) and then 2.8-3.3% through 2038, rising to 6.4% and 8.5% in the 2039-40 tail [S11 Table 15-5]. The 2027 exploration budget of US$11.4m [F37] is inside that allowance rather than capitalised. The 1H 2026 P&L ratio (10.6m on 30.9m, 34%) is not a run-rate: it carries listing costs on a half-year of ramp-up revenue.

flags.message: cannot re-price the last actual year: volume FY2025A
flags.justification: There is no last actual year to re-price: Pani achieved first gold production in February 2026 [S2 p.1], so FY2025A had no gold volume, no cash cost and no mine D&A to calibrate against - the pack's US$0.13m of FY2025 revenue is heavy-equipment rental to related parties [S11 p.196]. The calibration that can be run is against the only actual gold year, FY2026: 15,635 oz sold at the reported 9M ASP of US$4,306/oz [S2 Table, F11, F6] is about US$67m of revenue (the 1H share was US$30.9m [S3 p.8], so the arithmetic reconciles), at a cash cost of US$826/oz [F7]; the model's 0.96 realisation x the deck's US$4,493.75/oz and its US$826/oz FY2026E cost reproduce that unit economics. The engine's calibration block stays empty because the historical pack has no production basis, not because the forecast is unchecked.

flags.message: a.volume moves -26% from FY2026E to FY2040E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: The volume path is a mine-plan profile, not a drift: it falls 26% from FY2026E to FY2040E because the CPR produces 4,585 koz over 15 years, peaking at 545 koz in 2031 and tapering to 92 and 63 koz in 2039-40 as the reserve is worked out [S11 F17, F18]. Every year is taken from the CPR schedule, and the first two years match the company's own guidance (85-100 koz for 2026, "well above" 150 koz for 2027) [S2 F3, F4]. A flat volume is the wrong assumption for a finite orebody.

flags.message: a.cost_per_bcm moves +39% in real terms from FY2026E to FY2040E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: Unit cash cost rises from US$826/oz to US$1,218/oz because the fixed mining, processing and G&A base is spread over a falling denominator - 63 koz in 2040 against 505 koz in 2030. The CPR shows the same shape in its own numbers, with AISC excluding royalties rising from US$695/oz in 2031 to US$2,167/oz in 2040 [S11 Table 15-5, F21, F22]. The mid-life fall to US$484/oz is real operating leverage: the first CIL plant lifts throughput from 165 to 545 koz on a largely fixed cost base [S2 p.1, S11].

flags.message: a.da_unit moves -55% in real terms from FY2026E to FY2040E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: D&A per ounce falls 64% in real terms because it is depreciation of a fixed asset base spread over a rising volume, then a falling one: the CPR's D&A runs US$106.2m in 2027, US$169.2m in 2028 and US$59.2m by 2039 as the plant depreciates over the mine life [S11 Table 15-5, F23]. The CPR's 2040 figure of US$434.8m is the mine-closure provision unwinding, not productive depreciation, so it is normalised to US$300/oz here and the closure cash sits in capex_unit instead - which is why the series ends below where it starts.

flags.message: a.capex_unit moves -84% in real terms from FY2026E to FY2040E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: Capex intensity falls 87% because the build is front-loaded and then stops: the CPR spends US$296m of expansion capital in 2026 and US$722m in 2027 on the first CIL plant, then about US$20m a year of sustaining capital from 2028 [S11 Table 15-5, F24], against which the company has ordered the long-lead equipment and mobilised MCC15 and MCC6 [S2 p.1]. Holding US$3,520/oz of capex flat would imply the mine builds a new process plant every year of its life; the fallen intensity is the whole investment case.

flags.message: a.volume: bear 0.95 vs bull 1.13 is lopsided — mirror the shock or justify the asymmetry
flags.justification: The volume asymmetry is sourced, not a bias: the reserve statement is 5.2 Moz [F14] against the 4,585 koz the CPR plan mines [F17], so 615 koz - about 13% of the plan - is already in reserves and can be processed on the same infrastructure once the CIL surge capacity is used. The bull carries those ounces (x1.13) because they are stated reserves, while the bear still takes volume x0.95 for a CIL commissioning slip; mirroring the bull back to x1.05 would value 615 koz of stated reserve at zero, which MOST_LIKELY_BASE_CASE forbids. Costs, capex and gold are mirrored.

flags.message: balance-sheet cash restated at 2.01x the data pack: say why the pack is wrong
flags.justification: The pack's 30 June 2026 cash of US$62.1m is four months stale and predates two balance-sheet events: the ING gold prepayment of US$100m received on 28 September 2026 and the cash retained from the HKEX secondary listing [S2 p.12, F25, F29]. At 30 September 2026 cash and equivalents net of restricted cash were US$125m, which is 2.0x the pack figure. Debt is restated on the same date and basis (US$674m: finance lease 74, prepayment 100, Pani RCF 350 and EMAS RCF 150 fully drawn [F26-F30]); leaving the June numbers in place would value a company that has since drawn its facilities and sold forward gold.

flags.message: the DCF stops after 15 years while reserves last ~61 years at FY+1 volume: extend the horizon or justify the cut
flags.justification: The 15-year horizon follows the mine plan, not reserves divided by ramp-year output: the CPR processes 4,585 koz from 2026 to 2040 and the 5.2 Moz reserve statement is built on that 15-year plan [S11 F17, F18, F14]. Dividing 5.2 Moz by the depressed first-year volume of 85 koz produces a notional 61-year life that no disclosed plan supports - the first year is a ramp, not a run-rate. The rest of the reserve and resource base is expansion optionality (a second CIL plant and the 445 koz Kolokoa resource) with no published timetable or capex, so it is described in the report rather than discounted into the base case [S3 p.3].

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_life': 0.6, 'ev_ebitda': 0.3, 'pbv': 0.1}
flags.justification: The weight shift is the commodity template's method hierarchy rather than an opinion: the industry default is dcf_life 0.6 / ev_ebitda 0.3 / pbv 0.1, and the life-of-asset NAV at a through-cycle price carries 0.9 here because Pani is a single finite orebody with a published plan, no clean set of listed pure-play gold peers and a book value being rebuilt from a pre-production base [S11]. The engine in any case drops both multiples for lack of a peer set and own history, so the DCF carries effectively all of the target.
